claims.text: The diverse mechanical and thermoelastic behaviors of HfNbTaTiZr arise from residual internal stresses.
The proposed residual stresses are generated by thermal-expansion mismatch between distinct microstructural domains during processing.
Annealed HfNbTaTiZr contains incipient short-range-ordered or precipitate domains within a disordered high-entropy matrix.
Residual internal stresses modify the alloy's yield behavior.
Residual internal stresses modify the alloy's elastic moduli.
Residual internal stresses modify the alloy's creep resistance.
Changing the cooling rate after high-temperature annealing will systematically change the level of thermal-expansion-mismatch-induced residual stress.
Slow cooling produces greater residual thermal-stress buildup than rapid quenching.
Rapid quenching minimizes residual stresses arising from thermal-expansion mismatch.
Differential contraction creates localized tensile or compressive stresses at interfaces between emerging microstructural entities and the matrix.
Residual stresses pre-load the lattice.
Residual-stress preloading alters dislocation mobility.
Residual-stress preloading alters phase stability.
Residual-stress preloading alters the effective elastic response.
Residual stresses cause enhanced hardening after cold rolling and aging.
Slow-cooled samples will have higher elastic moduli from 293 to 1100 K than rapidly quenched samples.
Slow-cooled samples will have greater microhardness after cold rolling than rapidly quenched samples.
Slow-cooled samples will have lower tensile-creep rates at approximately 1250 °C than rapidly quenched samples.
Precipitation kinetics, grain-boundary chemistry, and processing-induced defects may also affect the measured mechanical responses.
The cited literature establishes that HEAs can contain nanoprecipitates, ordered solid-solution phases, and disordered solid-solution phases.
